claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was the most important theologian and biblical scholar of the early Greek church, born c. 185 in Alexandria, Egypt, and died c. 254 in Tyre, Phoenicia.
Origen was a Christian exegete and theologian who made copious use of the allegorical method in his commentaries and laid the foundations of philosophical theology for the church.
Origen's Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans is the oldest extant commentary on Romans, written around 246 CE.
The work was originally composed in Greek in Caesarea.
The commentary was one of Origen's longest and most mature works, and is the only commentary of Origen available in a coherent form from beginning to end.
Only fragments of the Greek archetype have survived.
Origen's admirer Rufinus of Aquileia translated the work into Latin around 406 CE.
Origen wrote the commentary to defend human freedom and oppose the natural predestinarian doctrine of Gnostic sects founded by Marcion, Valentinus, and Basilides.

These Gnostic schools relied heavily on texts from Paul, interpreted in isolation from the rest of Scripture, to deny free will and support the doctrine that salvation is determined by the nature one receives at birth, whether good or evil.

Origen defended the Church against the 'doctrine of natures'—the belief that all human beings are born with unalterable natures, either good or evil, and thus bound for either salvation or damnation, and that their conduct during this life cannot alter their destiny.
Provoked by Marcion's repudiation of the Old Testament, Origen emphasized the harmony between Gospel and Law.
Origen's exegesis predates the controversy between Augustine and Pelagius by 170 years, offering a striking perspective on Romans.
